You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failing test calls `StrBuilder.deleteAll("\n%BLAH%")` on a StrBuilder initialized with the string "\n%BLAH%\nDo more stuff\neven more stuff\n%BLAH%\n". The current bug report mentions that `StrBuilder.replaceAll` and `StrBuilder.deleteAll` can throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Looking at the `deleteAll` method code, it works as follows:
- It measures the length of the string to delete.
- If length > 0, it searches for occurrences of the string within the StrBuilder using `indexOf` starting at index 0.
- While an occurrence is found (index >= 0), it deletes the substring from that position using `deleteImpl`.
- Then it looks for the next occurrence of the string starting from the deleted position.

The `deleteImpl` method shifts characters left in the buffer (via System.arraycopy) and reduces the size by the length of the deleted string.

The `indexOf` method finds the position of the search substring starting at startIndex.

The problem likely arises when the `deleteAll` method is deleting multiple occurrences of a substring: after deleting the first occurrence, the buffer and size shrink. However, the next search for the string happens again at the same index, without accounting for the changed buffer length. This causes the `indexOf` method to search beyond the reduced bounds of the buffer, and when `deleteImpl` attempts a System.arraycopy operation with positions invalidated by a previously deleted substring, an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException occurs.

In particular, after the line `deleteImpl(index, index + len, len);` the size is already reduced by len. Yet on the next line, `index = indexOf(str, index);` tries to find the next occurrence starting at the same index, but the internal buffer and size have changed.

If the deleted substring occurred multiple times consecutively or near each other, starting the next search at the same index may cause the code to run past the new buffer size or miscalculate indices.

Thus, the root cause is that the `deleteAll` method does not adjust the starting index for the next search after deleting the substring, leading to an invalid array operation in `deleteImpl`. The fix is to ensure the subsequent search starts at an appropriate index to reflect the changed buffer state after deletion.

The test from the report demonstrates this with multiple occurrences of "\n%BLAH%" at the start and the end of the builder's content. The second delete call tries to find the next occurrence starting at the same index, leading to the out-of-bounds error.

Recent bug reports don't seem to relate directly to this substring deletion error but rather concern string utility functions and javadoc errors, so they don't add relevant information to this diagnosis. 

Therefore, the bug is in the `StrBuilder.deleteAll(String)` method's loop that calls `indexOf` after a deletion without adjusting the start index properly, causing `deleteImpl` to throw an `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
